title: Synodical letter: to ‘adore’ images is to kiss and love them—Greek prosechein/proskunein as embrace and strong love
source_text: XII. Consona sunt quae leguntur in epistola Synodica prima ad Augustos. Sunt autem haec, nempe Christi & sanctorum imagines, adorandae quoque, hoc est, exosculandae & amandae, idem enim significant haec, juxta antiquam Graeciae Dialecton. Nam prosechein, id est, adorare, & aspazesthai, id est, amplecti, & philein, id est, amare significat. Praepositio autem pros, intentionem significat desiderii, quemadmodum in proskunein. Unde concludit epistola vocem proskunein significare amplexum, & vehementem amorem. Tomi saepius allegati pag. 390.
pass_a_gloss: Consonant are the things which are read in the first Synodical epistle to the Augusti. But these are they: namely the images of Christ and of the saints are also to be adored, that is, to be kissed and loved, for these mean the same according to the ancient Dialect of Greece. For prosechein, that is, to adore, and aspazesthai, that is, to embrace, and philein, that is, to love, signify. But the preposition pros signifies the intention of desire, as in proskunein. Whence the epistle concludes that the word proskunein signifies embrace and vehement love. Tom. often cited, p. 390.
pass_b_english: The synodical letter equates ‘adoring’ images with kissing and loving them.
Greek usage (proskunein and kin) is pressed to mean embrace and strong affection, not latria.
